headline.main: Chip Challenges: The Munich Contribution to Apple's New iPhone 16
headline.social: Chip Challenges: The Munich Contribution to Apple's New iPhone 16

intro: With the iPhone 16e, Apple has launched a new middle-class device. The 5G chip it uses was largely developed in Munich. DER SPIEGEL spoke with those behind the novelty.
text:
Initially, Tim Cook’s comments about what Apple would be presenting were rather nebulous. Last week on X, he wrote: "Get ready to meet the newest member of the family.” It included the date: February 19. He didn’t need to say more. Almost everyone who knows anything about Apple was certain that the company would be introducing the new iPhone SE, 4th generation, a relatively affordable middleclass smartphone. Tech blogs had already begun speculating about the technical specs.
They were all wrong.
Instead of presenting the next phone in the SE series, which has always been a mixture of new and older technology, Apple presented a completely new device on Wednesday, the iPhone 16e. More modern than the SE, more expensive and with a new chip that Apple has never shown before.
More iPhone 16, Less iPhone SE
Equipped with the latest technology, such as the A18 chip from the iPhone 16, which is a key element of Apple Intelligence, as well as a 6.1-inch OLED display, it offers "the essential benefits of the iPhone 16 experience at the most affordable price,” iPhone manager Kaiann Drance said in an interview with DER SPIEGEL. It is, perhaps unsurprisingly, not as cheap as the last iPhone SE, which cost 519 euros when it was launched in 2022. The smallest version with 128 gigabytes (GB) of storage space costs 699 euros, just 150 euros less than an iPhone 15 currently costs at Apple. It is, in other words, anything but a bargain. The versions with 256 and 512 GB, of course, cost more.
But the price includes a more powerful camera than the iPhone SE. As with the iPhone 16, Apple calls it a "2-in-1” system, because by cutting out 12 megapixels from the center of a 48-megapixel image, it is possible to simulate the function of a 2x telephoto camera. The most important difference to the upper-class iPhone lies in its additional camera.
As has become standard, the 16e can be unlocked using Apple’s Face ID, relying on facial recognition instead of a fingerprint, and it has an action button that can be used to immediately call up a number of functions.
A "New iPhone Era”
It also, according to Drance, has the longest battery life of all iPhones that are equipped with a 6.1-inch screen. This is made possible by Apple’s C1 chip, which is being used for the first time in the iPhone 16e. The C1 is responsible for that part of the smartphone that only very few users will likely even notice: the mobile modem, responsible for mobile data connectivity.
Whether for phone calls, mobile web surfing, social media doomscrolling or checking emails, it is the C1 that establishes the connection when data needs to be downloaded or sent when on the move. It also offers GPS functions and can set up satellite connections when there is no reception.
Qualcomm Stress
Just how important the issue is for Apple became clear back in 2019. That year, the company acquired Intel’s smartphone modem development department for $1 billion. Numerous patents for mobile technologies, along with around 2,000 Intel employees – many of them in Munich – moved from Intel to Apple.
That same year, the company reached an agreement with chip maker Qualcomm, putting an end to several lawsuits against each other. One of those lawsuits involved Apple’s accusation that Qualcomm had been demanding excessive licensing fees for its mobile phone patents. Ultimately, the two companies agreed on a licensing deal valid for six years. They also signed supply contracts extending for several years for Qualcomm mobile modems, which have since been used in iPhones and iPads to connect the devices to mobile networks.
Apple agreed to the expensive deal because there were simply no alternatives. Intel was unable to deliver modems with the performance specs Apple was demanding and Apple was well aware that developing its own modem chip would take several years.
Investing in Munich
Since then, Apple has also invested billions in its Munich locations, including a 30,000 square meter (323,000 square foot) building for chip development on the central street of Karlstraße, just a stone’s throw from the main train station. Right next door, another building is being converted for Apple, and construction on a third site across the street has already begun. In the end, the Munich city center will be home to an Apple campus employing thousands of engineers.
The reason for the California-based company’s commitment to the Bavarian capital is clear: the availability of the most important resource for chip development – well-trained engineers. In an interview with DER SPIEGEL, Johny Srouji, head of Apple chip development, said: "When I hire, I hire the best team, whenever and wherever they are. And Germany proves to be a great place to hire good talent.”
He's not just referring to staff recruited from nearby Munich Technical University, as can be seen from the company’s numbers. Around 2,000 employees hailing from more than 40 countries are currently employed by Apple in Munich and they are closely networked with development teams in the U.S., Israel and elsewhere. But Srouji leaves no doubt as to how important the Munich team is to him. The team in Germany, he says, "was extremely key to developing, designing, testing, enabling and shipping this product.”
The fact that the development of chips which, to the outside observer, are merely responsible for linking to the network, requires so much labor and knowhow, has to do with the fact that such chips are, as Srouji points out, "complex technology.” In reality, they are not one single chip, but an assembly of several chips that are responsible for different tasks. One sends and receives signals, another codes and decodes data streams, and both digital and analog signals must be processed in parallel. And it is all held together with complex software architecture.
There are several reasons why Apple is prepared to invest billions of dollars to develop such a chip when the company could easily have continued buying them from Qualcomm. One of them is independence. In the 15 years since the company introduced its first proprietary iPhone chip, the A4, it has liberated itself from semiconductor suppliers in more and more areas. These days, chips developed in-house can be found in the company’s computers, smartphones, smartwatches and even headphones.
What the C1 Chip Can Do
By developing its own chips and linking them closely to its own software, Apple can shape systems in ways that would not be possible using components from other manufacturers. One example from the iPhone 16e: "The C1 and A18 are tightly integrated so they can transfer data quickly and efficiently,” says Apple manager Arun Mathias. By exchanging data with the main processor, the C1 knows what the user is currently doing with the device and can adapt to it.
As such, only those parts of the chips are activated that are required for a specific task, which allows for energy consumption to be controlled dynamically, says Mathias. As a result, the C1 chip "is the most power efficient modem that we’ve ever had in an iPhone.” Compared to the modems used in earlier iPhone generations, he says, "you can save 25 percent energy with the same usage” – a significant reason for the iPhone’s improved battery life.
An additional argument is likely lower costs, once Apple begins having its modem chips manufactured at TSMC virtually at cost instead of buying them from Qualcomm.
When Will That Become a Reality?
Johny Srouji compares the switch from Qualcomm chips to the C1 with the switch from Intel processors to the company’s own M chips in Mac computers. The C1 "is the first iteration. It is the start of a long-term strategy,” he says.
And, as he makes clear: "We developed it with the iPhone 16 in mind and for other products to follow.” Apple’s modem chip and its successors will thus likely be gradually introduced into iPads and future high-end iPhones. And perhaps – this is pure speculation – into MacBooks. Apple fans have been dreaming of a 5G MacBook for some time now.
Patience, though, is called for. As optimistic as the company is, the C1 will have to prove itself in the iPhone 16e over the coming months. It must be determined whether it really can deliver what it promises. Developers will then have an opportunity to make adjustments and incorporate improvements before it is potentially built into a top-of-the-line iPhone. For comparison, the transition from Intel to Apple chips in Mac and MacBooks took several years.
